DEPARTMENT 732 LAW AND MOTION RULINGS


Case Number: 23STCV01739    Hearing Date: June 29, 2026    Dept: 732

Alexander Montoya v. Philly Auto, Inc., et al. 

 

Monday, June 29, 2026 

 

 

 

CASE NUMBER: 23STCV01739 

 

UNOPPOSED 

___________________________________________________________________ 

 

Plaintiff Alexander Montoya’s Motion to Compel Compliance with Subpoena against Nonparty Mercedes Benz of Los Angeles. ___________________________________________________________________ 

 

Facts: This is an action for fraud and breach of warranty. The First Amended Complaint alleges as follows. Plaintiff Alexander Montoya (“Plaintiff”) purchased a 2020 Mercedes Benz A35 AMG from Defendant Philly Auto, Inc. based on express representations and warranties that the vehicle was being repaired to be in good condition for its eventual buyer. (FAC ¶¶ 9–11.) The vehicle contained or developed substantial defects contrary to the dealer’s representations, and they have been unable to fix the vehicle. (FAC ¶¶ 13–15.)  

Procedural History: Plaintiff filed the original Complaint on January 26, 2023, and filed the FAC on July 28, 2023, alleging eight causes of action: 

  1. Consumer Legal Remedies Act 

  1. Intentional Misrepresentation 

  1. Negligent Misrepresentation 

  1. Breach of Express Warranty 

  1. Failure to Promptly Repurchase 

  1. Breach of Implied Warranty of Merchantability 

  1. Unfair Competition 

  1. Vehicle Code § 11711 

Plaintiff filed the present motion to compel compliance with subpoena on June 18, 2026. No opposition has been filed.  

Analysis 

 

  1. MOTION TO COMPEL COMPLIANCE WITH SUBPOENA 

 

“If a subpoena requires the attendance of a witness or the production of books, documents, electronically stored information, or other things before a court, or at the trial of an issue therein, or at the taking of a deposition, the court, upon motion reasonably made by any person described in subdivision (b), or upon the court's own motion after giving counsel notice and an opportunity to be heard, may make an order quashing the subpoena entirely, modifying it, or directing compliance with it upon those terms or conditions as the court shall declare, including protective orders. In addition, the court may make any other order as may be appropriate to protect the person from unreasonable or oppressive demands, including unreasonable violations of the right of privacy of the person.” (Code Civ. Proc., § 1987.1, subd. (a).) 

Plaintiff Alexander Montoya (“Plaintiff”) seeks to compel nonparty Mercedes-Benz of Los Angeles (“MBLA”) to comply with a subpoena issued to it on February 13, 2025. (Savage Decl. ¶ 2.) The subpoena seeks documents related to MBLA’s service of the subject vehicle in this action or its communications with Defendant Philly Auto, Inc. (“Defendant”) regarding the same. (Savage Decl. Exh. 2.) The parties agreed to pause discovery while mediation was pending, and said mediation concluded on March 19, 2026, without settlement. (Savage Decl. ¶¶ 5–6.) Since then, no documents have been produced, no objection to the subpoena has been served, and no motion to quash has been filed. (Savage Decl. ¶¶¿7–8.)  

Plaintiff contends that the documents are necessary because MBLA was one of the entities charged with repairing the subject vehicle, and it is thus in possession of witnesses or other information bearing upon Plaintiff’s claims. (Motion at p. 2.) No opposition to the motion has been filed.  

Good cause appearing for the documents requested, and no opposition having been filed, the motion to compel compliance is GRANTED. Responsive documents shall be produced within 20 days of this order.

Case Number: 24STCV26948    Hearing Date: June 29, 2026    Dept: 732

TG Investments & Consulting, Inc. v. Barbara L. Anderson, et al. 

 

Monday, June 29,2025 

 

 

 

CASE NUMBER: 24STCV26948 

 

OPPOSED 

___________________________________________________________________ 

 

Defendant Coldwell Banker Residential Brokerage Company’s Demurrer and Motion to Strike Portions of the First Amended Complaint. ___________________________________________________________________ 

 

Facts: This is an action for negligence and misrepresentation. The Complaint alleges as follows. Plaintiff TG Investments & Consulting, Inc. (Plaintiff) purchased certain real property from Defendant Barbara L. Anderson (Anderson) in a transaction brokered through Defendant Coldwell Banker, escrowed through Defendant Granite Escrow & Settlement Services (Granite), and Defendant First American Title Company providing title services. (Complaint ¶¿11.) Before the sale, Defendants disclosed that the only encumbrance on the property was $61,547.19 owed to the City of Los Angeles for code violation penalties. (Complaint ¶ 13.) They did not disclose liens associated with prior city violations and demolition orders amounting to $223,000. (Complaint ¶ 15.)  

 

Procedural History: Plaintiff filed the Complaint on October 15, 2024, alleging seven causes of action: 

 

  1. Breach of Contract 

  1. Negligence 

  1. Negligent Misrepresentation 

  1. Intentional Misrepresentation 

  1. Breach of Fiduciary Duty 

  1. Breach of the Implied Covenant of Fair Dealing 

  1. Failure to Disclose 

 

Plaintiff filed the FAC on June 6, 2025, alleging the same causes of action.   

 

Defendant Coldwell Banker (“CB”) filed the present demurrer and motion to strike portions of the FAC on August 19, 2025. 

 

Plaintiff filed oppositions on June 15, 2026. 

 

CB filed replies on June 18, 2026. 

 

 

  

Analysis: 

  1. DEMURRER 

A demurrer should be sustained only where the defects appear on the face of the pleading or are judicially noticed. (Code Civ. Pro., §§ 430.30, et seq.) In particular, as is relevant here, a court should sustain a demurrer if a complaint does not allege facts that are legally sufficient to constitute a cause of action.¿(See id.¿§ 430.10, subd. (e).) As the Supreme Court held in Blank v. Kirwan (1985) 39 Cal.3d 311: “We treat the demurrer as admitting all material facts properly pleaded, but not contentions, deductions or conclusions of fact or law. . . . Further, we give the complaint a reasonable interpretation, reading it as a whole and its parts in their context.”¿(Id. at p. 318; see also Hahn. v. Mirda (2007) 147 Cal.App.4th 740, 747 [“A demurrer tests the pleadings alone and not the evidence or other extrinsic matters. Therefore, it lies only where the defects appear on the face of the pleading or are judicially noticed. [Citation.]”)  

 

“In determining whether the complaint is sufficient as against the demurrer … if on consideration of all the facts stated it appears the plaintiff is entitled to any relief at the hands of the court against the defendants the complaint will be held good although the facts may not be clearly stated.”  (Gressley v. Williams (1961) 193 Cal.App.2d 636, 639.) 

 

“A demurrer for uncertainty is strictly construed, even where a complaint is in some respects uncertain, because ambiguities can be clarified under modern discovery procedures.” (Khoury v. Maly’s of Cal., Inc. (1993) 14 Cal.App.4th 612, 616.) Such demurrers “are disfavored, and are granted only if the pleading is so incomprehensible that a defendant cannot reasonably respond.” (Mahan v. Charles W. Chan Insurance Agency, Inc. (2017) 14 Cal.App.5th 841, 848.) 

 

A demurrer should not be sustained without leave to amend if the complaint, liberally construed, can state a cause of action under any theory or if there is a reasonable possibility the defect can be cured by amendment. (Schifando v. City of Los Angeles, supra, 31 Cal.4th at p. 1081.) The demurrer also may be sustained without leave to amend where the nature of the defects and previous unsuccessful attempts to plead render it probable plaintiff cannot state a cause of action. (Krawitz v. Rusch (1989) 209 Cal.App.3d 957, 967.) 

 

Defendant Coldwell Banker Residential Brokerage Company (“CB”) demurrers to each cause of action pleaded against it on the grounds that, although Plaintiff T.G. Investments & Consulting Inc.’s (“Plaintiff”) Complaint is based on the failure to disclose a lien on property purchased by Plaintiff in the amount of $223,000.00, public records reveal that the lien was terminated the day after the close of escrow. (Demurrer at p. 8; RJN Exh. A.) As to particular claims, CB argues that the first cause of action for breach of contract and the sixth cause of action for breach of the covenant of fair dealing concern a purchase agreement to which CB was not a party; and that the third and fourth causes of action for negligent and intentional misrepresentation do not plead the representations at issue with particularity. (Demurrer at pp. 5–8.) 

 

Plaintiff in opposition argues that the demurrer is untimely, rests upon matter extrinsic to the First Amended Complaint (“FAC”), and that the FAC contains facts concerning other agreements and representations sufficient to attach liability to CB. (Demurrer at pp. 6–11.) 

 

CB in reply does not contest that the demurrer is untimely under Code of Civil Procedure §§ 430.40 and 430.41. (Reply at p. 2.) However, the decision to hear an untimely demurrer is within the court’s discretion. (Jackson v. Doe (2011) 192 Cal.App.4th 742, 749.) Plaintiff identifies no prejudice suffered from the tardy filing, and the late filing of the demurrer does not affect the defects in the FAC that the demurrer identifies, which if not challenged by demurrer may be challenged by a motion for judgment on the pleadings. (See Code Civ. Proc. § 438.)  

 

CB’s identification of a recorded termination of title does not afford it relief at the pleading stage, however. It is true that each cause of action is predicated upon damages suffered by Plaintiff as a result of the nondisclosure of a $223,000 lien held by the City of Los Angeles on the property at issue. (FAC ¶¶ 27–30, 38–42, 53–55, 62–66, 72–73, 83–84, 91–92.) This court may take judicial notice of the termination of this lien recorded by the City on August 14, 2024. (RJN Exh. A; Evid. Code § 452.) But this court cannot take judicial notice of CB’s contention that this extinguishment of the lien occurred on the day after the close of escrow, or that Plaintiff in fact suffered no damages as a result of the lien’s nondisclosure. (Motion at p. 4.) Thus the court cannot sustain the demurrer on the grounds that no damages were in fact suffered.  

 

However, CB is correct that the first, third, fourth, and sixth causes of action for breach of contract, intentional and negligent misrepresentation, and breach of the implied covenant of fair dealing. The first and sixth causes of action fail to allege both the predicate contracts and predicate misrepresentations upon which they are based. Contract claims, such as the first and sixth causes of action, are vulnerable to demurrer when “it cannot be ascertained from the pleading whether the contract is written, is oral, or is implied by conduct.” (Code Civ. Proc. § 430.10, subd. (g).) Here the only agreement alleged is the written purchase agreement, to which CB is not alleged to be a party. (FAC ¶ 25.) The sixth cause of action makes brief reference to an “agency agreement” with CB, but does not describe the nature of the contract or the terms CB violated. (FAC ¶ 75.) This is insufficient basis upon which to allege a contract claim.  

 

Likewise, the third and fourth causes of action for misrepresentation necessarily rely upon some affirmative misrepresentation made by CB. (See Graham v. Bank of America, N.A. (2014) 226 Cal.App.4th 594, 605 [elements of intentional misrepresentation];  National Union Fire Ins. Co. of Pittsburgh, PA v. Cambridge Integrated Services Group, Inc. (2009) 171 Cal.App.4th 35, 50 [elements of negligent misrepresentation].) But the FAC alleges no affirmative misrepresentations by CB or its agent — only the failure to disclose the lien on an Agent Visual Inspection Disclosure form. (FAC ¶¶ 50, 60.) Although Plaintiff argues that CB, as a broker and fiduciary, may be liable for a failure to disclose (Opposition at pp. 9–10), these theories are articulated in Plaintiff’s fifth and seventh causes of action for breach of fiduciary duty and failure to disclose, and do not permit the assertion of claims based on theories of affirmative misrepresentation when no such representations are alleged.   

 

Accordingly, the demurrer is SUSTAINED as to the first, third, fourth, and sixth causes of action for breach of contract, intentional and negligent misrepresentation, and breach of the implied covenant of fair dealing, with leave to amend. Any amended pleading shall be filed within 20 days of this order.  

 

  1. MOTION TO STRIKE 

Any party, within the time allowed to respond to a pleading, may serve and file a notice of motion to strike the whole or any part thereof. (Code Civ. Proc., § 435(b)(1)). The notice of motion to strike a portion of a pleading shall quote in full the portions sought to be stricken except where the motion is to strike an entire paragraph, cause of action, count or defense. (California Rules of Court Rule 3.1322.) 

The grounds for a motion to strike shall appear on the face of the challenged pleading or form any matter of which the court is required to take judicial notice. (Code Civ. Proc., § 437(a)). The court then may strike out any irrelevant, false, or improper matter inserted in any pleading and strike out all or any part of any pleading not drawn or filed in conformity with the laws of this state, a court rule, or an order of the court. (Code Civ. Proc., § 436.) When the defect which justifies striking a complaint is capable of cure, the court should allow leave to amend. (Perlman v. Municipal Court (1979) 99 Cal.App.3d 568, 575.) 

CB moves to strike the FAC’s prayer for attorney fees on the grounds that no statute or agreement is alleged to provide a basis for fees against CB. (Motion at p. 5.) CB also argues that Plaintiff fails to plead a basis for punitive damages. (Motion at pp. 5–7.)  

Punitive damages are allowed in non-contract cases when a defendant is guilty of “oppression, fraud, or malice . . . .” (Civ. Code § 3294, subd. (a).) The terms are defined as: 

  1. “Malice” means conduct which is intended by the defendant to cause injury to the plaintiff or despicable conduct which is carried on by the defendant with a willful and conscious disregard of the rights or safety of others. 

  1. “Oppression” means despicable conduct that subjects a person to cruel and unjust hardship in conscious disregard of that person's rights. 

  1. “Fraud” means an intentional misrepresentation, deceit, or concealment of a material fact known to the defendant with the intention on the part of the defendant of thereby depriving a person of property or legal rights or otherwise causing injury. 

(Civ. Code § 3294, subd. (c).) 

Something more than the mere commission of a tort is always required for punitive damages. (Taylor v. Superior Court (1979) 24 Cal.3d 890, 894.) Proof of negligence, gross negligence, or recklessness is insufficient to warrant an award of punitive damages. (Dawes v. Sup.Ct. (Mardian) (1980) 111 Cal.App.3d 82, 88–89.) Punitive damages may be recovered in an action for negligence or other nonintentional torts if the plaintiff pleads and proves that the defendant acted with the state of mind described as “conscious disregard” of the potential dangers to others. (Pfeifer v. John Crane, Inc. (2013) 220 Cal.App.4th 1270, 1299.) When malice is based on a defendant’s conscious disregard of Plaintiff’s rights, the conduct must be both despicable and willful. (College Hospital v. Superior Court (1994) 8 Cal.4th 794, 713 (“College Hospital”).) 

Plaintiff here alleges a viable claim for punitive damages based on allegations that CB intentionally failed to disclose known encumbrances upon the subject property in violation of its fiduciary duties. Although CB obliquely challenges these claims by its reference to the officially recorded termination of lien, as explained above, that termination of lien does not provide a basis for relief on demurrer or motion to strike.  

However, CB is correct that the FAC alleges no basis for its prayer for attorney fees. “Except as attorney's fees are specifically provided for by statute, the measure and mode of compensation of attorneys and counselors at law is left to the agreement, express or implied, of the parties; but parties to actions or proceedings are entitled to their costs, as hereinafter provided.” (Code Civ. Proc. § 1021.) Plaintiff here cites no statute or contractual basis to seek fees against CB, and does not address this point in its opposition. 

 

Accordingly, the motion to strike is GRANTED as to the prayer for attorney fees with leave to amend.   

 

 

 

 

 

Superior Court of California

BARBARA L. ANDERSON, et al.,

Defendant Coldwell Banker Residential Brokerage Company’s Demurrer and Motion to Strike Portions of the First Amended Complaint are SUSTAINED as to the first, third, fourth, and sixth causes of action for breach of contract, intentional and negligent misrepresentation, and breach of the implied covenant of fair dealing, with leave to amend, and GRANTED as to the prayer for attorney fees, with leave to amend. The demurrer is otherwise OVERRULED and the motion to strike DENIED. Any amended pleading shall be filed within 20 days of this order.

Case Number: 26STCP00229    Hearing Date: June 29, 2026    Dept: 732

Chatham Bend Holdings, LLC v. Amrish Patel., et al. 

 

Monday, June 29, 2026 

 

 

 

CASE NUMBER: 26STCP00229 

 

OPPOSED 

___________________________________________________________________ 

 

Defendant Amrish Patel’s Motion to Vacate Sister State Judgment ___________________________________________________________________ 

 

Facts: This is an action on a sister state judgment. The action is based on an application submitted by Plaintiff Chatham Bend Holdings, LLC (“Plaintiff”) upon a judgment entered on February 16, 2021, against Defendants Amrish Patel and Lab Development Group, LLC (“Defendants”) in Greenville County, South Carolina, in the amount of $366,832.88. (Application at p. 1.)  

Procedural History: Plaintiff filed the application on January 14, 2026. 

Judgment was entered pursuant to the application on January 14, 2026. 

A proof of service was filed indicating service of the notice of entry of judgment upon Defendants on February 2, 2026.  

Defendant Patel filed the present motion to vacate judgment on March 4, 2026.  

Plaintiff filed an opposition on June 15, 2026. 

Plaintiff filed a reply on June 22, 2026. 

Analysis 

 

  1. MOTION TO VACATE SISTER STATE JUDGMENT 

 

A sister state judgment entered in this state “may be vacated on any ground which would be a defense to an action in this state on the sister state judgment, including the ground that the amount of interest accrued on the sister state judgment and included in the judgment entered pursuant to this chapter is incorrect.” (Code Civ. Proc. §¿1710.40, subd. (a).)  

 

The defenses that may be asserted in a motion to vacate under section 1710.40 are not well defined. The Act itself does not specify the available defenses. However, the Law Revision Commission's comment to section 1710.40 lists certain “[c]ommon” defenses. It states: “Common defenses to enforcement of a sister state judgment include the following: the judgment is not final and unconditional (where finality means that no further action by the court rendering the judgment is necessary to resolve the matter litigated); the judgment was obtained by extrinsic fraud; the judgment was rendered in excess of jurisdiction; the judgment is not enforceable in the state of rendition; the plaintiff is guilty of misconduct; the judgment has already **334 been paid; suit on the judgment is barred by the statute of limitations in the state where enforcement is sought.” (Cal. Law Revision Com. com., 20 West's Ann. Code Civ. Proc. (2007 ed.) foll. § 1710.40, p. 385; see Traci & Marx Co. v. Legal Options, Inc. (2005) 126 Cal.App.4th 155, 158–159[23 Cal.Rptr.3d 685] (Traci & Marx).) 

 

(Casey v. Hill (2022) 79 Cal.App.5th 937, 976.) One available ground to challenge the sister state judgment is to argue that the other court’s  “exercise of personal jurisdiction violated due process.” (Id. at p. 960.)  

 

“The party moving under section 1710.40 to set aside the sister state judgment has “the burden to show by a preponderance of the evidence why it was entitled to relief.” (Conseco Marketing, LLC v. IFA & Ins. Services, Inc. (2013) 221 Cal.App.4th 831, 841.)  

 

Defendant Amrish Patel (“Defendant”) argues that he sister state judgment obtained against him by Plaintiff Chatham Bend Holdings, LLC (“Plaintiff”)  in South Carolina on February 16, 2021, and presently entered with this court, was obtained in violation of constitutional guarantees of due process because he was never served with process and lacked actual notice of the underlying action. (Patel Decl. ¶¶ 2–3.)  

 

Plaintiff in opposition contends that Defendant did not receive actual notice of the South Carolina action because service was made by publication pursuant to court order. (Opposition at p. 2; Segal Decl. Exhs. 1–3.)  

 

Defendant in reply argues that service by publication failed to comport with due process because the application materials do not support the conclusion that Plaintiff diligently attempted to serve Defendant by other means. (Reply at pp. 1–2.)   

 

“Consistent with the notions of fair play and due process, substituted service by publication is “a last resort” when “reasonable diligence to locate a person in order to give him notice before resorting to the fictional notice afforded by publication” has been exercised.” (Calvert v. Al Binali (2018) 29 Cal.App.5th 954, 963.) “If a creditor's identity is known or reasonably ascertainable, service by publication does not comply with the Fourteenth Amendment due process clause notice requirement—actual notice is constitutionally required. (Flores v. Kmart Corp. (2012) 202 Cal.App.4th 1316, 1330.) “If a defendant's address is ascertainable, a method of service superior to publication must be employed, because constitutional principles of due process of law, as well as the authorizing statute, require that service by publication be utilized only as a last resort.” (Watts v. Crawford (1995) 10 Cal.4th 743, 749 fn. 5.)  

 

The parties do not dispute whether Defendant had actual notice of the underlying South Carolina action. Plaintiff presents the affidavit of diligence supporting the application for service by publication in that action, signed on September 24, 2020, in which Plaintiff’s then-counsel stated as follows: 

 

I have reviewed publicly available documents on file with Greenville County but have been unable to locate Lab Development Group LLC a/k/a Lab Development Group (LDG) LLC and Armish Patel ("Publication Defendants"). This search has included a skip-trace of Publication Defendants, a review of circuit court records and deed records, and searches of reputable online search engines/websites in an attempt to locate Publication Defendants.  

 

(Segal Decl. Exh. 2 [Mitchell Decl. ¶ 4].) The declaration then describes four service attempts upon co-defendant Lab Development Group, LLC at three different addresses, and two service attempts upon Amrish Patel at an address on Providence Boulevard in Macon, Georgia, listed as Defendant’s “last known address.” (Segal Decl. Exh 2 [Mitchell Decl. ¶ 5.) The documents contain an affidavit of diligence by a process server, listing four attempts upon the Macon address without making contact with any individual residing there. (Segal Decl. Exh. 2.) The documents include two affidavits from a sheriff’s deputy upon the Macon address, who states in each that the defendants “have not lived here in at least 3 years.” (Ibid.)  

 

Plaintiff also submits a press-release from the FDIC Office of Inspector General discussing an apparent criminal conviction by Defendant in 2023 for crimes related to bank fraud. (Segal Decl. Exh. 5.) It is not apparent whether this evidence is admissible to impeach Defendant’s credibility. (See Evid. Code § 788 [describing when felony convictions are admissible].) Plaintiff also submits evidence of four other judgments entered against Defendant in Greenville County during the period from 2019 through 2020, three of which are evidently for “foreclosure.” (Segal Decl. Exh. 6.)  

 

Defendant  in reply contends that the evidence presented by Plaintiff in opposition does not demonstrate diligence in seeking to serve Plaintiff, or demonstrate that his location was not reasonably ascertainable. Defendant submits materials indicating that from about 2017 to potentially 2019, about a year before service was attempted in 2020, he was doing business as a doctor from an office on Patrick henry Parkway in McDonough, Georgia. (Supp. Patel Decl. Exhs. H–J.) The first two of these exhibits consist of a DEA registration dated January 31, 2017. (Supp. Patel Decl. Exh. H.) The second is a Henry County occupation tax certificate, seeking Defendant’s gross receipts for the period from October 2018 through September 2019, and listing his practice location as the same Patrick Henry Parkway address. (Supp. Patel Decl. Exh. I.) The same document lists his home address as being located in Stockbridge, Georgia. (Ibid.) That same Stockbridge address is listed as Defendant’s address in what is evidently an August 2017 Experian report. (Supp. Patel Decl. Exh. F.)1 Defendant finally submits an undated screenshot of what is evidently a web profile on a platform called “doximity,” listing his practice address as being once again Patrick Henry Parkway in MacDonough, Georgia. (Supp. Patel Decl. Exh. J.)  

 

The evidence does not permit a reasonable conclusion as to whether Plaintiff exercised reasonable diligence in attempting service upon Defendant at the Macon address, or whether Defendant’s location at this time was ascertainable. The declaration submitted in support of the application for publication described the Macon address as Defendant’s “last known address,” without elaboration, and did not describe in any detail the searches conducted to locate him. Plaintiff submits judgments taken against Defendnat in the same county near the same time, but the information provided does not disclose how service was accomplished or attempted against Defendant in these actions.  

 

Defendant’s evidence in reply, meanwhile, is largely unauthenticated except by Defendant’s attestation that the exhibits are “true and correct copies of records.” (Supp. Patel Decl. ¶ 2.)   Defendant does not explain how he comes to possess, for instance, in June 2026, a copy or a screenshot of an Experian report showing his own address as of 2017, or provide any explanation as to the origin of the screenshot of his “doximity” profile, including when the screenshot was taken, or whether it could have been observed during the pendency of the underlying action, when service was being attempted against him. 

 

Accordingly, supplemental briefing is required to permit a determination as to whether Defendant’s location was ascertainable at the time service by publication was requested in the underlying South Carolina action. The hearing on the motion is CONTINUED to permit the parties time to provide such briefing. Said briefs shall be filed within the time scheduled for the filing of oppositions under Code of Civil Procedure § 1005, subd. (b), in relation to the new hearing date.   

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

Superior Court of California 

County of Los Angeles 

Department 732 

 

CHATHAM BEND HOLDINGS, LLC.,  

Plaintiff 

v. 

AMRISH PATEL. et al., 

Defendants. 

  Case No.:  26STCP00229 

  Hearing Date: June 29, 2026 

 [TENTATIVE] RULING RE: 

Defendant Amrish Patel’s Motion to Vacate Sister State Judgment 

 

 

Hearing on Defendant Amrish Patel’s Motion to Vacate Sister State Judgment is CONTINUED to permit additional briefing by the parties as to whether Defendant’s location was ascertainable at the time service by publication was requested in the underlying South Carolina action. These supplemental briefs shall be filed within the time scheduled for the filing of oppositions under Code of Civil Procedure § 1005, subd. (b), in relation to the new hearing date.

Case Number: 26STCV11169    Hearing Date: June 29, 2026    Dept: 732

Nima Hefaz et al. v. Richard Hill, et al. 

 

Monday, June 29, 2026 

 

 

 

CASE NUMBER: 26STCV11169 

 

OPPOSED 

___________________________________________________________________ 

 

Plaintiff Nima Hefazi and Sheeva Zolghadr’s Motion to Compel Arbitration is GRANTED as to Defendants Rich Hill and Jordan Rudd,.  

___________________________________________________________________ 

 

Facts: This is an action for fraud and construction negligence. The Complaint alleges as follows. Plaintiffs Nima Hefazi and Sheeva Zolghadr (“Plaintiffs”) purchased property from Defendants Richard Hill and Jordan Rudd (“Sellers”), pursuant to disclosures that no renovations had taken place on the property except that was licensed and permitted according to applicable building codes. (Complaint ¶¶ 12–19.) Sellers in fact had conducted numerous renovations not in compliance with applicable codes or permits, and which shall cost Plaintiffs substantial sums to remediate. (Complaint ¶¶ 25–52.)  Defendants Rich Hill LLC and 8334 Kirkwood LLC are Defendants’ alter egos. (Complaint ¶ 5.) 

 

Procedural History: Plaintiffs filed the Complaint  on April 7, 2026, alleging seven causes of action: 

 

  1. Breach of Contract 

  1. Civil Code § 1102 

  1. Fraudulent Concealment 

  1. Fraud 

  1. Negligence 

  1. Negligence Per Se 

  1. Negligent Misrepresentation 

 

Plaintiff filed the present motion to compel arbitration on April 22, 2026. 

 

Defendants filed an opposition on June 12, 2026. 

 

Plaintiffs filed a reply on June 18, 2026. 

 

Analysis: 

  1. MOTION TO COMPEL ARBITRATION 

On petition of a party to an arbitration agreement to arbitrate a controversy, a court must order the petitioner and respondent to arbitrate the controversy if it determines the arbitration agreement exists, unless (1) the petitioner has waived its right to arbitrate; (2) grounds exist for the revocation of the agreement; or (3) “[a] party to the arbitration agreement is also a party to a pending court action or special proceeding with a third party, arising out of the same transaction or series of related transactions and there is a possibility of conflicting rulings on a common issue of law or fact.” (Code Civ. Proc., § 1281.2.)  

 

“[T]he party moving to compel arbitration bears the burden of establishing the existence of a valid agreement to arbitrate, and the party opposing arbitration bears the burden of proving by a preponderance of the evidence any fact necessary to its defense. The role of the trial court is to sit as a trier of fact, weighing any affidavits, declarations, and other documentary evidence, together with oral testimony received at the court's discretion, to reach a determination on the issue of arbitrability.” (Hotels Nevada v. L.A. Pacific Center, Inc. (2006) 144 Cal.App.4th 754, 758.) 

 

Plaintiffs Nima Hefazi and Sheeva Zolghadr (“Plaintiffs”) move to compel arbitration of their claims against Defendants Rich Hill, Jordan Rudd, Rich Hill LLC, and 8334 Kirkwood LLC (“Defendants”). Defendants Hill and Rudd (collectively “Sellers”) executed a purchase agreement with Plaintiffs on the property underlying the present action, pursuant to which they agreed to arbitrate “any dispute or claim in Law or equity arising between them out of this Agreement or any resulting transaction.” (Hefazi Decl. Exh. 1 at p. 14.)  

 

Although Defendants Rich Hill LLC and  8334 Kirkwood LLC (collectively “Entities”) are not signatories to the arbitration agreement, Plaintiffs argue that they may nonetheless be compelled to arbitrate by virtue of their status as alter egos of Defendant Rich Hill. (Motion at pp. 12–16.) Plaintiff is correct that arbitration agreements may be enforced against alter egos of a signatory party. (See Bouton v. USAA Casualty Ins. Co. (2008) 167 Cal.App.4th 412, 424 [noting permissibility of enforcement against nonsignatories “who are agents or alter egos of a signatory party or intended third party beneficiaries of an arbitration agreement.”].)  

 

A finding that a corporate entity is an alter ego of another requires findings: “(1) that there be such unity of interest and ownership that the separate personalities of the corporation and the individual no longer exist and (2) that, if the acts are treated as those of the corporation alone, an inequitable result will follow.” (Greenspan v. LADT, LLC (2010) 191 Cal.App.4th 486, 511.) In assessing the existence of a unity of interest, courts assess various factors including commingling of corporate and personal assets, disregard of corporate formalities, use of the same office or business locations, and others. (Id. at pp. 512–513.)  

 

Plaintiffs here do not seek a traditional alter ego determination against Defendants, by which the owner of a corporate entity is made liable for the wrongs of the corporation. Rather, Plaintiffs here seek “outside reverse veil-piercing,” by which outsiders to the corporation seek to hold corporations liable for the debts of their owners.  (See Curci Investments, LLC v. Baldwin (2017) 14 Cal.App.5th 214, 221 [“Rather than seeking to hold an individual responsible for the acts of an entity, reverse veil piercing seeks to satisfy the debt of an individual through the assets of an entity of which the individual is an insider.”].) It has been held that, while California does not generally permit application of the doctrine against a corporation of which a debtor is a shareholder, it may be applicable to limited liability companies of which a debtor is a member, such as Entities here. (Curci Investments, supra, 14 Ca.App.5th at p. 223.)  

 

Plaintiffs argue that a unity of interest exists between Defendant Hill and the Entities. Plaintiffs argue that Hill was the sole manager of both entities at the time the purchase agreement was signed in September 2024, that he lists as his personal address the same mailing addresses listed by the Entities, and that he holds them out as components of a larger development company called Hill Development Company. (Motion at pp. 12–13; Hefazi Decl. Exh. 7.) Plaintiff argues that Hill used the proceeds of the sale of the underlying property to Plaintiffs to purchase property now owned by 8334 Kirkwood LLC. (Motion at p. 15.)  

 

Defendants argue that Hill is not the sole member, or the majority member, of Defendant 8334 Kirkwood, LLC, and Hill denies using the proceeds of the underlying sale to purchase the property owned by the Kirkwood entity. (Opposition at pp. 7–8.)  Defendants note that the property owned by Kirkwood was purchased through a loan, the documents and grant deed for which were signed by co-managers who were not Hill, and listed an address for the entity one other than that listed by Hill personally. (Opposition at pp. 7–8.)  

 

Plaintiffs have not shown that application of the alter ego doctrine is warranted here, applied specifically in reverse veil-piercing fashion against Defendant Entities with respect to the present arbitration agreement. While Plaintiffs present authority for the proposition that such a doctrine may be applied in California, they have not presented any authority for the proposition that outside reverse veil-piercing may be applied to render a corporation subject to an arbitration agreement.  

 

Moreover, Plaintiffs have not satisfied the second element required of any alter ego finding, i.e. that application of the doctrine is necessary to avoid an “inequitable result.” (Greenspan, supra, 191 Cal.App.4th at p. 511.) Indeed, excluding Defendant Entities from the agreement would not even render the agreement unenforceable. Although Defendants argue that arbitration cannot be compelled against Sellers alone based on application of Code of Civil Procedure § 1281.2, subd. (c) (Opposition at pp. 10–13), this court cannot apply that statute because the arbitration agreement specifically disclaims any application of the California Arbitration Act:  

 

Enforcement of and any motion to compel arbitration pursuant to this agreement to arbitrate shall be governed by the procedural rules of the Federal Arbitration Act, and not the California Arbitration Act, notwithstanding any language seemingly to the contrary in this agreement.  

 

(Nefazi Decl. Exh. 1 at p. 14.) This language specifically embraces the procedural provisions of the FAA to the exclusion of the CAA. “In accordance with choice-of-law principles, the parties may limit the trial court's authority to stay or deny arbitration under the CAA by adopting the more restrictive procedural provisions of the FAA.” (Victrola 89, LLC v. Jaman Properties 8 LLC (2020) 46 Cal.App.5th 337, 345.)  

 

While the CAA permits a court to deny a motion to compel arbitration where “[a] party to the arbitration agreement is also a party to a pending court action or special proceeding with a third party, arising out of the same transaction or series of related transactions and there is a possibility of conflicting rulings on a common issue of law or fact” (Code Civ. Proc. § 181.2, subd. (c)), no similar provision exists in the FAA. (See Cronus Investments, Inc. v. Concierge Services (2005) 35 Cal.4th 376, 388.) Thus, while under the CAA Defendants might hope to defeat arbitration by noting the agreement’s partial applicability to only some of the parties here, Plaintiffs may nonetheless proceed to arbitrate their claims against Sellers, even if Entities are not so compelled, because the procedural rules of the FAA, specifically agreed to by the signatories, do not permit such discretion.  The FAA indeed requires that litigation be stayed if it involves an issue pending in arbitration: 

 

If any suit or proceeding be brought in any of the courts of the United States upon any issue referable to arbitration under an agreement in writing for such arbitration, the court in which such suit is pending, upon being satisfied that the issue involved in such suit or proceeding is referable to arbitration under such an agreement, shall on application of one of the parties stay the trial of the action until such arbitration has been had in accordance with the terms of the agreement, providing the applicant for the stay is not in default in proceeding with such arbitration. 

 

(9 U.S.C. § 3.) Plaintiffs indeed acknowledge in reply that they suffer no prejudice from arbitration against the Sellers alone, while the present action is stayed to permit decision on the “derivative” question of Entities’ alter ego liability once the arbitration concludes. (Reply at pp. 8–9.)  

 

Accordingly, Plaintiffs have not demonstrated that application of outside reverse veil-piercing with regard to the arbitration agreement is necessary to avoid an inequitable result. The arbitration agreement is enforceable against Sellers alone, irrespective of whether it is enforceable against Entities under Code of Civil Procedure § 1281.2, subd. (c). 

 

The parties have not been able to agree to an arbitrator, and ask this court to choose from different lists of potential arbitrators. Plaintiffs contend that Defendants have forfeited any say int eh process by refusing to participate prior to the present motion, while Defendants argue that Plaintiff’s proposed arbitrators are based in Northern California and charge higher rates for out-of-town services. (Motion at p. 16; Opposition at pp. 14-15.) Both parties, however, present arbitrators offered through JAMS. (Bryn Decl. ¶¶ 7–8; Motion at p. 8.)  

 

The FAA permits a court to appoint an arbitrator where the parties cannot agree:  

 

If in the agreement provision be made for a method of naming or appointing an arbitrator or arbitrators or an umpire, such method shall be followed; but if no method be provided therein, or if a method be provided and any party thereto shall fail to avail himself of such method, or if for any other reason there shall be a lapse in the naming of an arbitrator or arbitrators or umpire, or in filling a vacancy, then upon the application of either party to the controversy the court shall designate and appoint an arbitrator or arbitrators or umpire, as the case may require, who shall act under the said agreement with the same force and effect as if he or they had been specifically named therein; and unless otherwise provided in the agreement the arbitration shall be by a single arbitrator. 

 

(9 U.S.C. § 5.)  

 

The arbitration agreement here provides only for the parties to agree to an arbitrator, and does not provide a presumptively permissible selection or a method therefore. (Hefazi Decl. Exh. 1 at p. 14.) But while the parties cannot agree to an arbitrator, they agree that any such arbitrator may be provided through JAMS. And for its part, JAMS rules provide procedures for arbitrator selection. (See JAMS Comprehensive Arbitration Rules & Procedures, Rule 15 [“Arbitrator Selection, Disclosures, and Replacement”], available at <https://www.jamsadr.com/rules-comprehensive-arbitration#Rule-15>.) This court therefore need not select the particular arbitrator if the parties are in agreement concerning the permissibility of JAMS as an arbitration vendor.  Plaintiffs and Sellers are therefore directed to arbitrate this matter through JAMS in Los Angeles.   

 

Accordingly, the motion to compel arbitration is GRANTED as to Defendants Rich Hill and Jordan Rudd, and DENIED as to Defendants Rich Hill LLC and 8334 Kirkwood LLC. The present action is STAYED while the arbitration is pending. Plaintiffs, Hill, and Rudd are directed to arbitrate their dispute through JAMS in Los Angeles.
